result:
I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of urban life, and how cities create a particular kind of loneliness that's almost beautiful if you let yourself feel it properly.

---

There's a specific hour in every major city, somewhere between midnight and four in the morning, when the streets become something other than what they are during the day. The traffic lights keep their rhythm, but there's no one to obey them. A single bus might pass, carrying three or four passengers who stare out at the empty avenues with the hollow-eyed patience of people who have nowhere else to be. This is when the city reveals itself as a machine that keeps running whether anyone is watching or not, and there's something both terrifying and comforting in that knowledge.

I used to walk through these hours in Chicago, where I lived for several years in my twenties. I'd leave my apartment in Rogers Park and head south along the lakefront, past the closed beaches and the darkened marinas, the sailboats bobbing in their slips like sleeping animals. The city skyline would rise ahead of me, and I would feel the particular loneliness of being surrounded by millions of sleeping people, each one curled into their own warmth, their own dreams, their own accumulated griefs and small satisfactions.

This is the paradox that cities perfected long before the internet made it universal: absolute proximity combined with absolute separation. You can live in a building with two hundred other souls, share walls with them, hear their footsteps and their arguments and the particular cadence of their television preferences, and never learn their names. The coffee shop regular who orders the same thing every morning, the person who always gets on the train at your stop, the neighbor whose dog you recognize by the jingle of its collar—these are not strangers, exactly, but they're not acquaintances either. They occupy a category for which we have no good word, something like "familiar unknowns."

I think this is why people in cities develop such elaborate private rituals. The woman who arranges her morning commute to always pass the same bakery window, the man who has a specific bench in the park where he eats his lunch, the teenager who walks home a particular way to pass a house where someone they once loved lived—these are ways of making meaning in an environment that offers none inherently. The city is indifferent, so we write ourselves into it through repetition and attention.

There's a famous photograph by Vivian Maier, the Chicago nanny who shot thousands of rolls of film that were only discovered after her death, showing her own shadow stretched across a sidewalk. She's holding the camera at her waist, and her shadow has this strange elongated quality, almost like a separate being. I think about that image often because it captures something essential about urban selfhood: we are simultaneously the observer and the observed, the person casting the shadow and the shadow itself, never quite able to see ourselves whole.

The pandemic changed something in this dynamic, at least for a while. Those midnight walks became afternoon walks, and the streets were empty at hours when they should have been full. The familiar unknowns disappeared behind masks, then behind closed doors, then into the uncertain territory of remote work and changed routines. I found myself missing people I had never spoken to, the particular ensemble of my morning train car, the way the barista at my regular coffee shop would already start my order when I was still two customers back in line. These were not friendships, but they were a kind of social fabric, and I hadn't understood how much I relied on it until it frayed.

Now, in whatever we call this phase—post-pandemic, endemic, the new normal, or simply now—the old patterns are returning, but changed. Some people never came back to the office buildings downtown. Some businesses closed and others opened in their places. The city I walk through now is not the same city I walked through in 2019, though the streets have the same names, the lake the same restless motion. I find myself making new rituals, finding new familiar unknowns, but there's a consciousness to it now that wasn't there before. I know how fragile this all is.

What I'm trying to understand, I think, is whether this urban loneliness is a deficiency to be cured or a form in its own right, with its own possibilities. There's a freedom in being unknown, in the crowd's protective anonymity. You can reinvent yourself daily, or choose not to invent yourself at all, simply drift. The philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the flâneur, the urban wanderer who moved through the nineteenth-century arcades with no purpose but observation, and there's still something of that figure possible now, though the arcades have become coffee shops and the boulevards have become whatever streets you happen to find yourself on at the right hour.

But the flâneur was always a privileged figure, someone with the time and means to wander without obligation. The loneliness of the city hits differently when you're sleeping in a shelter, or working a third shift, or trying to raise children in a studio apartment. My midnight walks were a choice, not a necessity, and I don't want to romanticize a condition that for many people is simply suffering.

Still, I return to those hours, that feeling. The city as a sleeping giant, breathing in the rhythm of its own infrastructure. The self as both more and less significant than it seems in daylight, one consciousness among millions, temporarily awake in the shared darkness. There's a kind of love possible in this, I think—not the love of specific others, but a diffuse affection for the whole impossible enterprise of human gathering, all these lives stacked and pressed together, each one as real and as urgent to its owner as your own is to you.

I don't know if this is wisdom or just another way of making peace with isolation. Probably it's both, probably it's neither, probably it's just what I have, walking through the hours when the city belongs to no one and therefore, briefly, to whoever is there to claim it with their attention. The traffic light changes, empty. The bus passes, nearly empty. I keep walking, one familiar unknown to myself, making my path through the dark.
